interest: U.S. firms freely sold aircraft and munitions technology to Japan in the 1930s.
overview: This file consists of the U.S. Department of State's master docket sheets and purport register (Form DS-46) for decimal file 894.113 ('Regulations Governing Firearms, Ammunition, Explosives - Japan') spanning 1930 through 1937, along with an associated 1932 case sheet concerning the Waterbury Farrel Foundry and Machine Company. Rather than containing original correspondence, the file serves as a comprehensive administrative register of incoming and outgoing diplomatic despatches, telegrams, interdepartmental communications, and corporate inquiries regarding the export, sale, transit, and regulation of arms, ammunition, aircraft, and war materials to Japan during the escalating Far Eastern crisis. The entries detail numerous requests by American manufacturers—such as Sperry Gyroscope, Curtiss Aeroplane, Pratt & Whitney, and Lockheed—for authorization to export weapons, aviation equipment, and manufacturing licenses to Japanese firms including Mitsui and Mitsubishi. Additionally, the docket traces the debates surrounding proposed U.S., British, and League of Nations arms embargoes following Japanese military operations in Manchuria and Shanghai, consistently reflecting the official stance of the State, War, and Navy Departments that commercial munitions sales remained legally unrestricted absent specific congressional embargo legislation, provided they did not compromise classified military secrets.

subfiles.about: Master purport register and docket sheets recording diplomatic communications, interdepartmental memoranda, and inquiries regarding firearms, munitions, aircraft technology, and arms embargo proposals relating to Japan from 1930 to 1937.
subfiles.summary: This 14-page register (Sheets 1–15, Form DS-46) catalogues documents in State Department decimal file 894.113 and related cross-referenced files concerning firearms, explosives, aircraft manufacturing rights, and war materials destined for Japan. It traces commercial inquiries from major American manufacturers—such as Sperry Gyroscope, Curtiss Aeroplane, Pratt & Whitney, and Lockheed—seeking approval to sell munitions, patrol boats, and aircraft engines to Japanese firms including Mitsui and Mitsubishi. The entries also document high-level diplomatic deliberations regarding proposed U.S., British, and League of Nations arms embargoes during the Manchurian crisis and Shanghai conflict, highlighting the U.S. position that commercial exports were legally unrestricted without congressional legislation. In addition, the register records diplomatic monitoring of Japanese domestic arms control legislation and foreign arms shipments to Japan originating in Europe and Latin America.
